analysis.one_liner: Removes federal restrictions that limit the ATF's ability to trace guns, inspect dealers, and enforce firearms laws.
analysis.headline: No action since its November 19, 2025 introduction: the bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no vote scheduled, and its 9 supporters are all House Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The AIM Act would strip out roughly a dozen budget riders, many known as the Tiahrt amendments, that currently stop the ATF from sharing gun-tracing data with police, keeping and searching dealer records, requiring gun dealers to physically count their inventory, and inspecting dealers more than once a year. It would also make it easier to revoke a gun dealer's federal license for breaking firearms laws, changing the standard from 'willful' violations to 'knowing' ones. The bill was introduced in November 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities affected by gun violence and the police who investigate shootings. The bill would let the ATF share trace data with local law enforcement, keep background-check records long enough to catch people who lied to buy a gun, search records from dealers that have gone out of business, and inspect problem dealers more often.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes limits on using firearms trace data, letting investigators use gun-tracing information to map and solve gun crime rather than being restricted to a single case.
It ends the rule requiring federal background-check records to be destroyed within 24 hours, so records can be retained long enough to audit checks and prosecute people who illegally obtained a gun.
It lets the ATF require gun dealers to conduct physical inventories, inspect dealer records more than once a year, and search the computerized records of dealers that have gone out of business.

It makes it easier to deny or revoke a federal firearms license by requiring only a 'knowing' violation of firearms law instead of a 'willful' one, and it limits the scope of new evidence dealers can raise when appealing a revocation.

analysis.who_pays: Gun dealers, gun importers, and the broader firearms industry. Dealers would face mandatory inventory checks, more frequent inspections, easier license revocation for violations, and loss of current protections keeping their records from being centralized and searched by the ATF.

drawbacks.text: The bill lowers the bar for revoking a gun dealer's license from 'willful' to 'knowing' violations and eliminates the dealer's right to a fresh review of their case in court, which raises fair-process concerns for small dealers facing revocation.

Removing the limits on trace data, FOIA disclosure, and electronic retrieval of dealer records means more federal retention and searching of gun-related records, which gun-rights groups have long argued edges toward a federal registration database; courts have never definitively resolved how far these powers reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real but indirect: better data, recordkeeping, and dealer oversight give police more tools to solve and prevent gun trafficking crimes, and law-abiding dealers are unaffected by rules aimed at violators. The costs fall on the firearms industry in extra compliance burden, and the due-process changes for dealers (knowing instead of willful violations, no de novo review) are a genuine trade-off. On balance, the bill strengthens enforcement of laws already on the books rather than creating new restrictions on gun owners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee on November 19, 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since; Congress is still in session, so it has not died yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Beyer (D-VA) introduced the ATF Improvement and Modernization Act of 2025 (AIM Act) on November 19, 2025, with Reps. Raskin, Titus, and Norton joining as original sponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced; the committee has held no markup or vote on it.
The bill has 8 Democratic cosponsors in addition to its sponsor, and no Republican support in the record.

The bill works entirely by repealing or amending provisions, mostly in annual appropriations acts, that currently restrict what the ATF may do with trace data, dealer records, background-check records, and inspections, and by changing the license-revocation standard in 18 U.S.C. 923.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill parked in committee, the current restrictions stay in place, so gun dealers and the firearms industry are better off so far; communities waiting for stronger enforcement tools have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, gun dealers and the firearms industry

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original sponsors at introduction.

against.what_they_did: Held the bill with no markup, hearing, or vote since its November 19, 2025 referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken, but all nine sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats, with no Republican support in the record.

industries.note: Dealers would face mandatory physical inventory checks, more frequent compliance inspections, easier license revocation for knowing violations, and loss of protections against centralized searching of their records. Better-policed dealer files help law enforcement catch gun trafficking that moves crime guns into communities.

The bill lets the ATF again deny import applications for certain shotguns and curio-and-relic firearms that current riders protect, restoring discretionary import limits that were stripped out in recent appropriations acts.

The record-keeping and trace-data expansions are the kind of federal firearms-record authority these groups have spent decades blocking through appropriations riders, making this bill a reversal of their long-standing position.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to committee this late in a first session, with only Democratic support and no committee action after introduction, rarely reach the floor on their own; the realistic paths forward are a Judiciary markup next session or the provisions being folded into a larger appropriations or gun-policy package. Absent one of those, the bill is likely to expire in committee at the end of this Congress.
